bib.title: LEAP: Supercharging LLMs for Formal Mathematics with Agentic Frameworks

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "LEAP: Supercharging LLMs for Formal Mathematics with Agentic Frameworks" (LLM-in-Lean Environment Agentic Prover), Po-Nien Kung, Linfeng Song, Dawsen Hwang, ... Quoc V Le, Thang Luong, Tomas Pfister, Nanyun Peng (Google Cloud AI Research / DeepMind). arXiv:2606.03303v2, 3 Jun 2026, preprint.

COVERAGE: All 24 of 24 pages read (70,980 chars). Body pp.1-11 in full, references pp.12-15 skimmed, appendices A-C pp.16-24 read (Lean statements and worked artifacts, no extra results tables). I did not read the note beyond its header and opening paragraphs (about 2,500 chars); it has no existing mention of LEAP/kung (grep found none). Not a scanned PDF; the extraction is clean apart from stripped spaces in the abstract and math symbols.

CLAIMS
1. LEAP, using only a general LLM (Gemini-3.1-pro) plus the Lean compiler as verifier, solves all 12 Putnam 2025 problems.
 number: 12/12 (100%). Baselines: Gemini-3.1-pro 0%, Goedel-Prover-V2-32B 0%, Hilbert 33.3%, Aristotle 75.0%.
 setup: Table 2. Baselines Gemini and Goedel are pass@128; Hilbert, Aristotle and LEAP are rollout=2. Hilbert rollouts were capped at 7 days.
 quote: "LEAP successfully solves all 12 Putnam 2025 problems, improving the benchmark solve rate from 0% via direct formalization to 100% with our agentic framework."
 where: p.7, section 4.1
2. On Lean-IMO-Bench (60 problems), LEAP scores 83.3% on Basic and 56.7% on Advanced. Aristotle scores 76.7% and 20.0%, Hilbert 36.6% and 6.6%, one-shot Gemini-3.1-Pro 20.0% and 3.3%.
 setup: Table 4. Gemini and Goedel are pass@128; the others are rollout=2. Geometry stays near zero for every method (LEAP 16.7% Basic, 12.5% Advanced).
 quote: "LEAP achieves the highest overall solve rates, scoring 83.3% on the Basic set and 56.7% on the Advanced set."
 where: p.8
 Note: the abstract says "from below 10% to 70%" and "48% ... IMO system". The intro says "under 10% to 70%, surpassing specialized ATP models (5%) and Aristotle (48%)". These are probably the overall average over both sets, and they do not match Table 4 directly. Table 4 gives LEAP (83.3+56.7)/2 = 70.0 and Aristotle (76.7+20.0)/2 = 48.35. Quote the Table 4 per-set figures, not the abstract's 70% and 48%, unless you state the derivation.
 quote: "LEAP boosts the one-shot formal solve rate of general-purpose LLMs from below 10% to 70%, notably surpassing the 48% bench-marksetbyaspecialized, gold-medal-caliberIMOsystem."
 where: abstract, p.1
3. A compiler-feedback loop helps a general model but not a specialized prover. Gemini-3.1-Pro goes from 20.0% (one-shot pass@128) to 36.6% (iterative pass@1 with up to 20 revision steps). Goedel-Prover-V2-32B goes from 10.0% to 6.6%.
 setup: Table 5, Lean-IMO-Bench Basic set. The two settings use different sampling budgets (128 samples against 1 initial attempt plus 20 revisions).
 quote: "Goedel-Prover-V2-32B does not benefit from this feedback loop, while Gemini-3.1-pro improves substantially from20.0%to36.6%."
 where: p.9, section 5.1
4. A compiler pass is not enough. A syntactically valid sketch can contain a useless decomposition, so an LLM reviewer is added as a second verification layer. Without it on Putnam A5, the agent fails even after 8 rollouts. With it, A5 was solved in 2 rollouts.
 setup: a single-problem ablation (Putnam 2025 A5, the hardest case and the longest runtime). One problem only, so anecdotal.
 quote: "Removing the LLM-based decomposition reviewer causes the agent to fail even after eight rollout attempts."
 where: p.10, section 5.3
 Failure mode (Fig. 3): the Lean sketch is formally admissible, but the proposed subgoal is "syntactically identical to the original statement". Without semantic review "this duplicate lemma is treated as a new step, causing the agent to repeat the same unproductive decomposition until its search budget is exhausted."
5. The reviewer checks three things: whether subgoals are relevant, whether they make the problem easier, and whether they offer a plausible route to completion. It acts as a search filter that triggers backtracking.
 number: none
 quote: "This planning-level review is crucial for complex goals, where a Lean sketch can be syntactically valid while introducing subgoals that are ill-posed or no simpler than the original statement."
 where: p.5, section 2.5
6. Verification constrains what the agent may write. A proof sketch may contain `sorry` only in the newly proposed lemma statements. This keeps the AND-OR semantics: once all children are proved, the parent is proved. A DAG state writer also checks acyclicity before committing an update.
 number: none
 quote: "the main theorem body issorry-free, while sorry placeholders are permitted only in the newly proposed lemma statements."
 where: p.4, section 2.2
7. Persistent DAG memory (shared lemma nodes, memoization) improves results over a naive tree with the same workflow. The tree variant scores 73.3% Basic and 40.0% Advanced. The full DAG scores 83.3% and 56.7%. The tree variant still beats Hilbert (36.6% and 6.6%).
 setup: Table 6, Lean-IMO-Bench.
 quote: "The full DAG version further improves performance from 73.3% to 83.3% on the Basic set and from 40.0% to 56.7% on the Advanced set"
 where: p.9, section 5.2
8. Informal reasoning ability does not transfer to formal output without a verifier loop. In the one-shot baseline, Gemini 3.1 Pro gets Pass@128 20.0% (Basic) and 3.3% (Advanced), with Avg@128 of 4.6% and 0.2%. Natural-language proofs from Gemini 2.5 Pro (Pass@1, human-reviewed) reach 55.2% and 17.6%. Giving a correct informal proof barely helps formal translation.
 quote: "Providing a correct informal proof in the Formal Proof Translation task also yields little improvement, with Pass@128 unchanged and only a marginal gain in Average@128."
 where: p.6, Table 1
9. The compute cost is large and varies by problem. Putnam LLM calls per problem range from 46 (b2) to 3.0k (a5). Active DAG nodes range from 8 to 211. Proof length reaches 2.0k lines.
 quote: "LLM Calls 71 304 963 1.4k 3.0k 1.0k 116 46 98 87 239 161"
 where: p.8, Table 3
10. Case study: a verified Lean proof of a subproblem of Knuth's Hamiltonian decomposition of even-order Cayley graphs (cycle of length m^2 for Color 2). It is over 5000 lines of Lean 4, and the informal argument spans about 20 pages. A second case, Erdős 457, was reproduced.
 setup: only the subproblem, not the full open problem. The "Erdős 457" case is described as "already resolved". No cost or time is given.
 quote: "ultimately synthesizing over 5000 lines of rigorous Lean 4 code to complete the formal proof for this subproblem."
 where: p.11, section 6

LIMITS
- Hilbert is bounded to 7 days per rollout and is described as having exponential complexity, O((n·b)^d) with d=10. Hilbert's low scores may partly reflect that cap.
- Aristotle is closed source. A footnote says an unofficial report has it at 10/12 on Putnam, while this paper measured 9/12. Axiom and Numina (closed) are not reproduced.
- The reviewer ablation covers one problem (A5). The sample is small (60 problems plus 12), and the rollout count is only 2.
- Baselines use unequal budgets (pass@128 against rollout=2), so budget-matched comparisons are not shown. No cost in dollars or tokens is reported beyond LLM-call counts.
- Only Gemini-3.1-pro is used as the backbone. The hybrid with specialized provers is left unexplored.
- Search is a simple DFS with backtracking. The authors name branch prioritization and compute allocation as future work.
- Geometry is near zero for every method.
- Lean-IMO-Bench problems are IMO-level and elementary, so results may not transfer to modern theory-heavy mathematics.
- The paper is from Google, with no outside replication. The authors say they contacted the vals.ai ProofBench leaderboard several times without a reply.

BUILDS ON
- Lean Blueprint tool (Massot; used in the Fermat's Last Theorem formalization)
- "Draft, sketch, and prove" (Jiang et al., 2023)
- Hilbert (Varambally et al., 2025)
- Aristotle (Achim et al., 2025)
- LeanSearch (Gao et al., 2024)
- Lean (Moura and Ullrich, 2021)
- IMO-ProofBench / IMO-Bench (Luong et al., 2025)
- Goedel-Prover-V2 (Lin et al., 2026)
- Hubert et al., 2026 (AlphaProof)
- Not credited for the reviewer idea as such. The paper only says the reviewer suggests "LLMs may also serve as heuristic evaluators".

CODE
- Sketch contract (p.19, Appendix C): "a proof sketch may contain sorry placeholders only for these explicitly proposed lemmas. Thus, a verified proof sketch defines a valid decomposition: once all referenced proposed lemmas are later proved, the current goal is also proved."
- Fig. 3 degenerate-decomposition pattern (p.10): a "Proposed subgoal (syntactically identical to the grandparent goal)" is `lemma card_perms_a_eq_card_perms_b ... := by sorry`.

FIGURES
- Fig. 1, p.3: LEAP workflow. The path is direct formalization with revision, then on failure blueprint, formal sketch, Lean verifier, LLM reviewer, then DAG state writer or reader. It shows two verifiers in one loop (a hard compiler check and a soft LLM review), with ACCEPT/REJECT/REVISER arrows.
- Fig. 2, p.5: example AND-OR DAG for Putnam A6.
- Fig. 3, p.10: Lean code for the unproductive decomposition without the reviewer, which is the best single illustration of "compiler-valid but useless".

FIT TO NOTE (observations only)
- This is evidence for the note's claim that the model's own "done" needs an external check. Here the external check is a deterministic compiler plus an LLM reviewer for what the compiler cannot judge.
- It also bears on loop detection and when to stop: the reviewer-less run repeats a cyclic decomposition until the budget is gone.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions found. The abstract's 70% and 48% figures are not given in any table (see claim 2). Abstract spacing is garbled. The first tool outputs were truncated in the tool display, so I read the persisted full text. The Read output also appended the note's text after the references; that is not part of the paper.
